extracted.intended_audience: students and practitioners of social science, political philosophy, and scientific method
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for selecting and applying proper methods in sociological/political inquiry, distinguishing mistaken approaches and recommending a concrete deductive method with verification and suitable scope. Emphasizes how to form useful generalizations about social phenomena.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rejection of the Chemical (experimental) Method for complex social phenomena
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'Chemical Method'—seeking to determine the effect of a single cause by subtracting the effects of other causes as in elementary chemistry—is a gross misconception when applied to political/social phenomena.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Experimental/chemical-style subtraction is ineffective because we cannot subtract the effect of all but one cause; verification by experiment only confirms conclusions already suggested by general laws. Anti-pattern: insisting on exhaustive experimental subtraction before accepting a priori reasoning about a single cause.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid the Geometrical (single-premise deductive) Method
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'Geometrical' method treats social science like geometry—deducing from one or a few immutable principles as if no conflicting causes could modify results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is erroneous because social phenomena always involve numerous coexisting causes whose effects can conflict or modify one another. Anti-pattern examples: building political theory solely on a single principle (e.g., 'government founded on fear' or 'men act only from self-interest') and treating that as sufficient to explain all social phenomena.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concrete Deductive Method: deduce from many premises
rubrics_metrics.description: Sociology must be deductive not after the model of geometry but after the model of more complex physical sciences—deduction from many premises (the Concrete Deductive Method).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Infer the law of each social effect from the laws of the several causes on which it depends, compounding their tendencies. Use astronomy and natural philosophy as analogues. Recognize that deduction must take account of multiple co-operant causes rather than single-cause deductions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verification: collate deductive conclusions with observation (a posteriori corroboration)
rubrics_metrics.description: Verification—comparing a priori deductions with concrete phenomena or empirical laws—is an essential constituent of a concrete deductive science.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The concurrence of a priori reasoning and a posteriori observation is the ground of confidence. Verification can come after deduction or the order can be inverted (derive provisional laws from experience, then connect them to principles by a priori reasoning). It remedies limitations of pure deduction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expect tendencies, not precise predictions
rubrics_metrics.description: Deductive sociology can yield statements of tendencies ('this cause will tend to produce X unless counteracted') but cannot reliably produce precise positive predictions about amounts or exact outcomes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tendencies are valuable for guidance and policy-making even if not infallible. Do not demand infallible foresight from sociological deduction—use it to surround policy with beneficial tendencies and to prepare precautions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Frame general propositions as hypothetical and specify assumed circumstances
rubrics_metrics.description: All general propositions in sociological deduction are, strictly speaking, hypothetical: grounded on a suppositious set of circumstances and true only insofar as those circumstances (and no unaccounted modifiers) apply.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make explicit the set of circumstances on which a theorem depends; if those circumstances match a real society and no omitted causes modify outcomes, conclusions hold. Anti-pattern: presenting context-specific conclusions as universal laws without stating assumptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit the complexity of hypothetical combinations
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid building extremely complex hypothetical combinations of many concurrent causes because uncertainty accumulates rapidly and soon deprives conclusions of value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Restrict deductive generalization to classes of social facts immediately influenced principally by a few causes. When more concrete truth is needed, increase the number of individualizing circumstances incrementally to reduce error, but be aware of rapidly growing uncertainty as causes are compounded.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for intermixture of laws and the social 'consensus'
rubrics_metrics.description: Social phenomena are characterized by an 'intermixture of laws' and a 'consensus' whereby every part of the social state influences every other; nothing in one part is entirely independent of the rest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that any cause's effect spreads through society, interacts with different agencies, and produces feedbacks; two societies will rarely exhibit identical effects of the same cause. Hence analysis must consider the wider social condition and reciprocal influences rather than treating phenomena in isolation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Study distinct branches separately when immediate causes differ
rubrics_metrics.description: Different species of social facts are in the main dependent, immediately and in the first resort, on different kinds of causes; therefore distinct (though not independent) branches of sociological speculation are justified.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Create separate departments (e.g., Political Economy for phenomena mainly arising from pursuit of wealth) to handle intricate analysis of a subset of causes, while allowing for later adjustment when other societal circumstances interfere. Anti-pattern: pretending a single branch's principles suffice for all social phenomena.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use allowances but do not mistake partial systems for complete science
rubrics_metrics.description: Constructing a theory from a few agencies and treating it as a complete scientific treatment is unphilosophical; allowances for omitted factors are not a substitute for including them when necessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While theorists may prudently apply allowances when using simplified premises (and such simplifications can be practically useful), one must not present a partial framework as the whole science. The superstructure cannot reliably compensate for insufficient foundations.
